title: What is a “homeschooling family”?
author: Michael McShane
summary: Michael McShane uses the misused word factoid, something that sounds true but is not, to challenge the assumption that families can be neatly sorted as public, private, charter, or homeschooling families. New research by Albert Cheng, Angela Watson, and Matt Lee finds that 53 percent of families with one homeschooled child send another child to a traditional school, and his team's 2026 Schooling in America Survey found 28 percent of parents have moved a child between sectors. McShane draws three lessons: parents, including homeschoolers, are far more pragmatic than ideological; their choices often reflect constraints such as cost, lotteries, and logistics rather than desires; and large numbers of families are up for grabs if a school meets their needs. He concludes that neither public nor private schools are guaranteed market share, and that competitive pressure in a pluralistic system should push all schools to improve.
points: McShane lists common education factoids, such as declining K-12 funding, learning styles, and the agrarian calendar.
Fifty-three percent of families with one homeschooling child send another child to a traditional school.
Parents rank practical reasons such as location, peers, safety, and academics above religious or moral instruction.
Barriers like distance, transportation, and juggling drop-offs constrain families even when choice exists.
School choice does not guarantee enrollment for any sector; schools must perform to attract families.
quotes: Education is full of factoids. For example: K-12 funding has declined over the years. Children have different learning styles. Schools let out for summer due to “the agrarian calendar.” All of these statements feel true. All are false.
They find that 53% of families that have one child homeschooling send at least one other child to a traditional school.
First, parents (including homeschooling parents) are far less ideological than stereotypes might suggest. Parents are pragmatic and want schooling environments that work for their children.
Second, parents’ choices often reflect constraints over desires. No one wants their child to be in a school where they are being bullied, but often parents are stuck there.

This has implications for public school supporters, who sometimes throw their hands up and pretend like opening the door of school choice means kids will desert public schools and never come back. That is not true. Do better and kids will come back (or never leave in the first place).
The fact that families’ choices are malleable and that families mix and match educational environments is good news for those of us who think that pluralism is good.
